newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei ends year's final session flat.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei ends year's final session flat.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's benchmark Nikkei 225 index ended the final session of 1996 on Monday little changed, after recouping early losses brought on by the yen's weakening against the dollar and fears that trade related to margin expiry would weigh down the index, brokers said.
The Nikkei 225 ended 7.69 points or 0.04 percent lower at 19,361.35, after slipping to 19,108.50 at one stage during the two-hour session. Its March futures fell 100 points to 19,300.
"Sentiment was glum to begin with and it was aggravated further by the yen's tumble to the 116 yen to the dollar level," said Masaaki Higashida, a strategist at Nomura Securities.

But market participants fervently hoping that the Nikkei average would end on a favourable tone pushed the index up in the final minutes of trade, leading it into backwardation, with the futures price lower than the spot price, brokers said.

"There were jitters that the Nikkei average would be battered by an avalanche of margin trade-related selling," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said. "But there had been heavy selling last week so the impact was not very damaging today."
Turnover totalled 149 million shares, with advancing issues outnumbering decliners by 596 to 453, with 199 issues unchanged.
Other indices managed to end the year on positive ground, with the TOPIX up 4.14 points or 0.28 percent at 1,470.94. The Nikkei 300 was up 0.92 point or 0.33 percent at 280.26.
The second section index was up 3.72 points or 0.20 percent at 1,824.46 with a turnover of 5.25 million shares, little changed from Friday's volume of 5.08 million.
Brokers said that despite the Nikkei's last-minute recovery, the market was unlikely to start 1997 trading on January 6 on an optimistic note.

"The indices finished higher, but the despondent atmosphere which has hammered stocks lower recently has not changed and probably won't change during the holidays," said Seiki Orimi, a Dai-ichi Securities analyst. "The outlook on the economy is bleak, holding back investors lacking in confidence."

The Nikkei's feeble finale was in contrast with its highstepping entry into 1996. It had leapt on the year's first day of trade on January 4, adding nearly 750 points to finish at 20,618.00, then the highest close since September 2, 1994.
But after peaking on June 26, when it hit a four-and-a-half year closing high of 22,666.80, it ran out of steam.

It slumped to this year's closing low on Christmas Eve at 19,161.71 as the economy's faltering recovery depressed investors. Soon afterwards it crashed past the 19,000 threshold for the first time in over a year.
Brokers said the market was shocked by the 1997 draft budget, which contains a tax rise of nearly seven trillion yen and a delay in a corporate tax cut.

The market mood was blackened by the yen's sudden slide to a 44-month low against the dollar last week. The yen fell further against the dollar on Monday to 116.18 yen at one stage, a low in Tokyo since March 1993.

"The biggest concern now that the market knows that the economy is not going to be rosy next year is the estimate of how heavy the burden of foreign investor selling will be," a broker at a "Big Four" brokerage said.
Recently battered Yaohan Japan Corp soared as buy-backs pushed it up 57 yen to 556 in volume of 5.467 million, making it the most heavily traded issue on the Tokyo bourse.

Global blue-chips were sought after, with Sony Corp climbing 20 yen to finish at 7,590. Semiconductor equipment maker Advantest Corp, seen as a blue-chip laggard, exceeded its high for the year during the session after gaining 80 yen, but fell back to close 40 yen higher at 5,430.
Sega Enterprises Ltd, which revised its group earnings forecast down, lost 150 yen to close at 3,900.
By sector, fisheries, iron and steel, warehouses, real estate and shipbuilding led gainers. Oil, services, communications equipment, land transport and transport equipment headed the losers.
